P1● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

A round tabletop has diameter 49 cm. Its area is: (Use π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​.)

area =πr2= \pi r^2=πr2 with r=diameter2r = \dfrac{\text{diameter}}{2}r=2diameter​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: the formula needs the radius.

The radius 24.5 cm is used.
This uses the diameter 49 cm as the radius.
This is the circumference, 227×49\dfrac{22}{7} \times 49722​×49 — a length.
This is 2πr22\pi r^22πr2, twice the area.

Given: diameter 49 cm; π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​. Asked: the area.

Concept used: area =πr2= \pi r^2=πr2 with r=diameter2r = \dfrac{\text{diameter}}{2}r=2diameter​ (Topic 1). Why it applies: the formula needs the radius.

  1. 1

    r=492=24.5r = \dfrac{49}{2} = 24.5r=249​=24.5 cm.

  2. 2

    Area =227×24.5×24.5=227×600.25=1886.5= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 24.5 \times 24.5 = \dfrac{22}{7} \times 600.25 = 1886.5=722​×24.5×24.5=722​×600.25=1886.5 cm².

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ The radius 24.5 cm is used.
    • (b) ✘ This uses the diameter 49 cm as the radius.
    • (c) ✘ This is the circumference, 227×49\dfrac{22}{7} \times 49722​×49 — a length.
    • (d) ✘ This is 2πr22\pi r^22πr2, twice the area.

  3. Check: 14×7546=1886.5\dfrac{1}{4} \times 7546 = 1886.541​×7546=1886.5 — halving the radius quarters the area ✔.

  4. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Squaring the diameter. Halve it first.

l=θ360×2πrl = \dfrac{\theta}{360} \times 2\pi rl=360θ​×2πr (Topic 2). Why it applies: the arc is the fraction 36360=110\dfrac{36}{360} = \dfrac{1}{10}36036​=101​ of the circumference.

This is one tenth of the area, 110×3850\dfrac{1}{10} \times 3850101​×3850 — the area formula used for a length.
This uses 36180\dfrac{36}{180}18036​; a full turn is 360°.
One tenth of the circumference.
This is the perimeter of the sector, 22+35+3522 + 35 + 3522+35+35; only the arc was asked.

Given: r=35r = 35r=35 cm; θ=36°\theta = 36°θ=36°. Asked: the arc length.

    Circumference =2×227×35=220= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 = 220=2×722​×35=220 cm.

    • (b) ✘ This uses 36180\dfrac{36}{180}18036​; a full turn is 360°.

P3● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

Find the perimeter of a quadrant of a circle of radius 21 cm. (Use π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​.)

Full solution

Given: quadrant; r=21r = 21r=21 cm. Asked: the perimeter.

Concept used: a quadrant is a 90° sector; perimeter =2r+l= 2r + l=2r+l (Topic 2). Why it applies: the boundary is two radii and the arc.

  1. 1

    Arc =14×2×227×21=14×132=33= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 21 = \dfrac{1}{4} \times 132 = 33=41​×2×722​×21=41​×132=33 cm.

  2. 2

    Perimeter =21+21+33=75= 21 + 21 + 33 = 75=21+21+33=75 cm.

  3. Check: the perimeter (75 cm) is more than the arc (33 cm) and less than the whole circumference plus a diameter ✔.

  4. Answer 75 cm

    Common trap: Answering 33 cm — the arc alone.

segment = sector − triangle (Topic 3). Why it applies: the segment is the sector without △OAB.

This is the whole sector — the triangle was not taken away.
This is the triangle, not the segment.
This adds the triangle to the sector.
Sector minus triangle.

Given: r=21r = 21r=21 cm; θ=90°\theta = 90°θ=90°. Asked: the minor segment.

P7● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

The minute hand of a table clock is 6 cm long. Find the area it sweeps in 40 minutes. (Use π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14.)

Full solution

Given: r=6r = 6r=6 cm; 40 minutes; π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14. Asked: the area swept.

Concept used: 6° per minute; area of a sector (Topic 2). Why it applies: the hand is a radius turning about the centre.

  1. 1

    Angle =40×6°=240°= 40 \times 6° = 240°=40×6°=240°.

  2. 2

    Area =240360×3.14×6×6=23×113.04=75.36= \dfrac{240}{360} \times 3.14 \times 6 \times 6 = \dfrac{2}{3} \times 113.04 = 75.36=360240​×3.14×6×6=32​×113.04=75.36 cm².

  3. Check: 40 minutes is two thirds of an hour, and 240360=23\dfrac{240}{360} = \dfrac{2}{3}360240​=32​ ✔.

  4. Answer 75.36 cm²

    Common trap: Using 40° — about 12.56 cm², far too small for two thirds of the clock face.

P8● FoundationMCQ · 1 markOriginal

Through what angle does the hour hand of a clock turn from 12 noon to 4 p.m.?

the hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours, so 30° per hour (Topic 2). Why it applies: it is the hour hand, not the minute hand.

30° per hour for 4 hours.
This uses the minute hand's 6° per minute as if it were per hour.
This takes 1° per hour.
This turns 240 minutes straight into 240°.

Given: from 12 noon to 4 p.m. (4 hours). Asked: the angle turned by the hour hand.

Concept used: the hour hand turns 360° in 12 hours, so 30° per hour (Topic 2). Why it applies: it is the hour hand, not the minute hand.

  1. 1

    4×30°=120°4 \times 30° = 120°4×30°=120°.

    Reasoning for each option:

    • (a) ✔ 30° per hour for 4 hours.
    • (b) ✘ This uses the minute hand's 6° per minute as if it were per hour.
    • (c) ✘ This takes 1° per hour.
    • (d) ✘ This turns 240 minutes straight into 240°.

  2. Check: from 12 to 4 is a third of the way round the face, and 360°3=120°\dfrac{360°}{3} = 120°3360°​=120° ✔.

  3. Answer (a)

    Common trap: Mixing up the hour hand (0.5° per minute) and the minute hand (6° per minute).
P9● FoundationVery short answer · 1 markOriginal

A wheel of radius 28 cm rolls along a straight path for 352 m. How many complete turns does it make? (Use π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​.)

Full solution

Given: r=28r = 28r=28 cm; distance 352 m. Asked: the number of turns.

Concept used: one turn = one circumference; both lengths in the same unit (Topic 1). Why it applies: the wheel rolls without slipping.

  1. 1

    Circumference =2×227×28=176= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 176=2×722​×28=176 cm.

  2. 2

    Distance =352×100=35 200= 352 \times 100 = 35\,200=352×100=35200 cm.

  3. 3

    Turns =35 200176=200= \dfrac{35\,200}{176} = 200=17635200​=200.

  4. Check: 200×176=35 200200 \times 176 = 35\,200200×176=35200 cm =352= 352=352 m ✔.

  5. Answer 200 turns

    Common trap: Dividing 352 (m) by 176 (cm) — the answer 2 is far too small.

P12●● StandardShort answer · 2 marksOriginal

A chord of a circle of radius 16 cm subtends 90° at the centre. Find the perimeter of the minor segment. (Use π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14 and 2=1.41\sqrt{2} = 1.412​=1.41.)

Full solution

Given: r=16r = 16r=16 cm; θ=90°\theta = 90°θ=90°. Asked: the perimeter of the minor segment.

Concept used: perimeter of a segment = chord + arc; at 90° the chord is r2r\sqrt{2}r2​ (Topic 3). Why it applies: △OAB is right-angled at O, so AB2=162+162AB^2 = 16^2 + 16^2AB2=162+162.

  1. 1

    Chord AB=162+162=162=16×1.41=22.56AB = \sqrt{16^2 + 16^2} = 16\sqrt{2} = 16 \times 1.41 = 22.56AB=162+162​=162​=16×1.41=22.56 cm.

  2. 2

    Arc =14×2×3.14×16=25.12= \dfrac{1}{4} \times 2 \times 3.14 \times 16 = 25.12=41​×2×3.14×16=25.12 cm.

  3. 3

    Perimeter =22.56+25.12=47.68= 22.56 + 25.12 = 47.68=22.56+25.12=47.68 cm.

  4. Check: the arc is longer than the chord ✔.

  5. Answer 47.68 cm

    Common trap: Arc + two radii (25.12+32=57.1225.12 + 32 = 57.1225.12+32=57.12 cm) — that is the perimeter of the sector.

major segment = circle − minor segment (Topic 3). Why it applies: the chord cuts the circle into these two pieces.

P15●● StandardTrue/False with justification · 2 marksOriginal

True or false? Give a reason. "The area of a sector of a circle of radius 5 cm and angle 72° is 15.7 cm." (Use π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14.)

Full solution

Given: r=5r = 5r=5 cm; θ=72°\theta = 72°θ=72°; π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14. Asked: is the statement correct?

Concept used: area of a sector; areas are in square units (Topics 1, 2). Why it applies: the statement gives a number and a unit.

  1. 1

    Area =72360×3.14×5×5=15×78.5=15.7= \dfrac{72}{360} \times 3.14 \times 5 \times 5 = \dfrac{1}{5} \times 78.5 = 15.7=36072​×3.14×5×5=51​×78.5=15.7.

  2. 2

    The number is right, but an area is measured in cm², not cm.

  3. Check: the arc of this sector is 15×2×3.14×5=6.28\dfrac{1}{5} \times 2 \times 3.14 \times 5 = 6.2851​×2×3.14×5=6.28 cm, so 15.7 cannot be a length on this sector; 15.7 is the area, so its unit must be cm² ✔.

  4. Answer False as written — the area is 15.7 cm².

    Common trap: Marking it true because the number matches. The unit is part of the answer.

Full solution

Given: r=35r = 35r=35 cm; 7 equal sectors. Asked: the area of one sector.

Concept used: n equal sectors share the circle equally: each is 1n\dfrac{1}{n}n1​ of it (Topic 2). Why it applies: the sectors are equal.

    Circle =227×35×35=3850= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 35 \times 35 = 3850=722​×35×35=3850 cm².

    Each sector =38507=550= \dfrac{3850}{7} = 550=73850​=550 cm².

  4. Answer 550 cm²

    Common trap: Dividing by 6 (as if 7 sectors had 6 gaps) — about 641.67 cm².

P17●● StandardShort answer · 3 marksOriginal

A goat is tied at one corner of a field in the shape of an equilateral triangle of side 20 m, with a rope 7 m long. Find (a) the area it can graze and (b) the area of the field it cannot graze. (Use π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​ and 3=1.73\sqrt{3} = 1.733​=1.73.)

Full solution

Given: equilateral field, side 20 m; rope 7 m at a corner. Asked: grazed and ungrazed areas.

Concept used: the grazed region is a sector with the corner's angle, 60° (Topic 4); area of an equilateral triangle 34a2\dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4}a^243​​a2 (Topic 1). Why it applies: the rope is shorter than the sides.

  1. 1

    (a) Grazed =60360×227×7×7=1546=773≈25.67= \dfrac{60}{360} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 7 \times 7 = \dfrac{154}{6} = \dfrac{77}{3} \approx 25.67=36060​×722​×7×7=6154​=377​≈25.67 m².

  2. 2

    Field =34×202=1003=173= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{4} \times 20^2 = 100\sqrt{3} = 173=43​​×202=1003​=173 m².

  3. 3

    (b) Not grazed =173−773≈147.33= 173 - \dfrac{77}{3} \approx 147.33=173−377​≈147.33 m².

  4. Check: the field's height is 103≈17.310\sqrt{3} \approx 17.3103​≈17.3 m, more than 7 m, so the sector fits ✔.

  5. Answer (a) about 25.67 m² (b) about 147.33 m²

    Common trap: Using a quadrant (90°). The corner of an equilateral triangle is 60°.

In Fig 11.3, a square is inscribed in a circle of diameter d and another square is circumscribing the circle. Is the area of the outer square four times the area of the inner square? Give reasons for your answer.

(Fig. 11.3, described: a circle with a small square inside it, its corners on the circle, and a larger square outside it, its sides touching the circle.)

Full solution

Given: circle of diameter d; inner and outer squares. Asked: is outer = 4 × inner?

Concept used: inner square: diagonal = d; outer square: side = d (Topic 5). Why it applies: corners on the circle / sides touching it.

  1. 1

    Inner square: area =d22= \dfrac{d^2}{2}=2d2​ (half the diagonal squared).

  2. 2

    Outer square: area =d2= d^2=d2.

  3. 3

    d2=2×d22d^2 = 2 \times \dfrac{d^2}{2}d2=2×2d2​ — twice, not four times.

  4. Check: d = 10: inner 50, outer 100 ✔.

  5. Answer No. The outer square's side equals the inner square's diagonal, so its area is twice the inner square's.

    Common trap: Thinking "side doubles" — the side grows by 2\sqrt{2}2​, not 2.

Given: a rhombus with its corners on a circle of area 1256 cm²; π=3.14\pi = 3.14π=3.14. Asked: the rhombus's area.

Concept used: quick reminder (Class 9): a parallelogram whose corners lie on a circle is a rectangle, so this rhombus is a square; its diagonals are diameters (Topic 5).

  1. 1

    3.14r2=12563.14 r^2 = 12563.14r2=1256, so r2=400r^2 = 400r2=400 and r=20r = 20r=20 cm.

  2. 2

    Both diagonals =40= 40=40 cm.

  3. 3

    Area =12×40×40=800= \dfrac{1}{2} \times 40 \times 40 = 800=21​×40×40=800 cm².

  4. Check: a square of diagonal 40 has side 20220\sqrt{2}202​ and area 800 ✔.

  5. Answer 800 cm²

    Common trap: Assuming the side is 40 cm.

E60●●● AdvancedShort answer · 3 marksNCERT Exemplar Ch 11, Ex 11.4 Q17

Find the area of the shaded region given in Fig. 11.20.

(Fig. 11.20, described: a shaded square of side 14 cm with an unshaded "flower" in the middle: a small square with a semicircle on each of its four sides; each semicircle's outer edge is 3 cm from the side of the big square.)

Full solution

Given: big square 14 cm; 3 cm gaps; π=227\pi = \dfrac{22}{7}π=722​. Asked: big square − flower.

Concept used: the flower is a small square of side a with four semicircles of diameter a; its width is 2a2a2a (Topic 5). Why it applies: the semicircles stick out a2\dfrac{a}{2}2a​ on each side.

  1. 1

    Width of the flower =14−3−3=8= 14 - 3 - 3 = 8=14−3−3=8 cm =2a= 2a=2a, so a=4a = 4a=4 cm and each semicircle has radius 2 cm.

  2. 2

    Flower =4×4+4×12×π×22=16+8π= 4 \times 4 + 4 \times \dfrac{1}{2} \times \pi \times 2^2 = 16 + 8\pi=4×4+4×21​×π×22=16+8π cm².

  3. 3

    Shaded =196−16−8π=(180−8π)= 196 - 16 - 8\pi = (180 - 8\pi)=196−16−8π=(180−8π) cm² =180−1767≈154.86= 180 - \dfrac{176}{7} \approx 154.86=180−7176​≈154.86 cm².

  4. Check: 2+4+2=82 + 4 + 2 = 82+4+2=8 ✔ and 3+8+3=143 + 8 + 3 = 143+8+3=14 ✔.

  5. Answer (180−8π)(180 - 8\pi)(180−8π) cm² ≈154.86\approx 154.86≈154.86 cm²

    Common trap: Taking the small square's side as 8 cm (the whole flower's width).

C1 — Case: the Pookalam designs●● StandardCase/source-based · 4 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Areas Related to Circles, Case Study 3

(Pictures, described: Design I — a circle with an equilateral triangle ABC inside it, all three corners on the circle, and small coloured triangles in the parts between. Design II — a square ABCD holding 9 equal round flower designs in 3 rows of 3, touching each other and the sides.)

Pookalam is the flower bed or flower pattern designed during Onam in Kerala. It is similar as Rangoli in North India and Kolam in Tamil Nadu. During the festival of Onam, your school is planning to conduct a Pookalam competition. Your friend who is a partner in competition, suggests two designs given below. Observe these carefully.
Design I: This design is made with a circle of radius 32cm leaving equilateral triangle ABC in the middle as shown in the given figure.
Design II: This Pookalam is made with 9 circular design each of radius 7cm.
Refer Design I:

  1. The side of equilateral triangle is

a) 12312\sqrt{3}123​ cm b) 32332\sqrt{3}323​ cm c) 48cm d) 64cm

  1. The altitude of the equilateral triangle is

a) 8 cm b) 12 cm c) 48cm d) 52cm
Refer Design II:

  1. The area of square is

a) 1264 cm² b) 1764 cm² c) 1830 cm² d) 1944 cm²

  1. Area of each circular design is

a) 124 cm² b) 132 cm² c) 144 cm² d) 154 cm²

  1. Area of the remaining portion of the square ABCD is

a) 378 cm² b) 260 cm² c) 340 cm² d) 278 cm²

Full solution

Given: Design I: r=32r = 32r=32 cm; Design II: 9 circles of radius 7 cm in a 3 × 3 square. Asked: five values.

Concept used: each side of the triangle is a chord subtending 120° at the centre (Topic 3: chord =r3= r\sqrt{3}=r3​, OM=r2OM = \dfrac{r}{2}OM=2r​); circle area (Topic 1). Why it applies: the three equal sides share 360° at O.

  1. 1

    Part 1: side =323= 32\sqrt{3}=323​ cm → b).

  2. 2

    Part 2: the altitude from A passes through O and meets BC at its mid-point M: AO+OM=32+322=48AO + OM = 32 + \dfrac{32}{2} = 48AO+OM=32+232​=48 cm → c).

  3. 3

    Part 3: three plates across: side =3×14=42= 3 \times 14 = 42=3×14=42 cm; area =1764= 1764=1764 cm² → b).

  4. 4

    Part 4: 227×49=154\dfrac{22}{7} \times 49 = 154722​×49=154 cm² → d).

  5. 5

    Part 5: 1764−9×154=1764−1386=3781764 - 9 \times 154 = 1764 - 1386 = 3781764−9×154=1764−1386=378 cm² → a).

  6. Check: altitude of an equilateral triangle =32×323=48= \dfrac{\sqrt{3}}{2} \times 32\sqrt{3} = 48=23​​×323​=48 ✔.

  7. Answer Part 1 b) · Part 2 c) · Part 3 b) · Part 4 d) · Part 5 a)

    Note on the official key: the bank's key (1 b, 2 c, 3 b, 4 d, 5 a) is correct.

    Common trap: Part 1: taking the side as the diameter (64 cm). A chord that subtends 120° is r3r\sqrt{3}r3​.

C2 — Case: the brooches (parts 1, 2, 3 and 5)●● StandardCase/source-based · 4 marksCBSE Mathematics Class X Case Study Question Bank, Areas Related to Circles, Case Study 4 (parts 1, 2, 3 and 5)

(Pictures, described: Brooch A — a circle divided into 8 equal sectors by 4 diameters. Brooch B — a silver disc with a gold ring round it. A photograph of a silver brooch.)

A brooch is a small piece of jewellery which has a pin at the back so it can be fastened on a dress, blouse or coat. Designs of some brooch are shown below. Observe them carefully.
Design A: Brooch A is made with silver wire in the form of a circle with diameter 28mm. The wire used for making 4 diameters which divide the circle into 8 equal parts.
Design B: Brooch b is made two colours_ Gold and silver. Outer part is made with Gold. The circumference of silver part is 44mm and the gold part is 3mm wide everywhere.
Refer to Design A

  1. The total length of silver wire required is

a) 180 mm b) 200 mm c) 250 mm d) 280 mm

  1. The area of each sector of the brooch is

a) 44 mm² b) 52 mm² c) 77 mm² d) 68 mm²
Refer to Design B

  1. The circumference of outer part (golden) is

a) 48.49 mm b) 82.2 mm c) 72.50 mm d) 62.86 mm

  1. A boy is playing with brooch B. He makes revolution with it along its edge. How many complete revolutions must it take to cover 80π mm?

a) 2 b) 3 c) 4 d) 5

(Part 4 of this case is left out: its official key is wrong — see the note in the solution.)

Full solution

Given: Brooch A: diameter 28 mm, 4 diameters; Brooch B: silver circumference 44 mm, gold 3 mm wide. Asked: four values.

Concept used: circumference; 8 equal sectors of 45°; ring radii; revolutions (Topics 1, 2). Why it applies: each piece is a circle, sector or ring.

  1. 1

    Part 1: circumference =227×28=88= \dfrac{22}{7} \times 28 = 88=722​×28=88 mm; 4 diameters =112= 112=112 mm; total =200= 200=200 mm → b).

  2. 2

    Part 2: 18×227×14×14=6168=77\dfrac{1}{8} \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 14 \times 14 = \dfrac{616}{8} = 7781​×722​×14×14=8616​=77 mm² → c).

  3. 3

    Part 3: silver radius: 2×227×r=442 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times r = 442×722​×r=44, so r=7r = 7r=7 mm; outer radius =7+3=10= 7 + 3 = 10=7+3=10 mm; circumference =2×227×10≈62.86= 2 \times \dfrac{22}{7} \times 10 \approx 62.86=2×722​×10≈62.86 mm → d).

  4. 4

    Part 5: one revolution =2π×10=20π= 2\pi \times 10 = 20\pi=2π×10=20π mm; 80π20π=4\dfrac{80\pi}{20\pi} = 420π80π​=4 → c).

  5. Check: Part 1: 8 sectors need only 4 diameters, since each diameter makes two radii ✔.

  6. Answer Part 1 b) · Part 2 c) · Part 3 d) · Part 5 c)

    Note on the official key: parts 1, 2, 3 and 5 are keyed correctly (b, c, d, c). Part 4 asks for "the difference of areas of golden and silver parts" and is keyed 51 (that is, 51π mm²). That is the gold ring's area, π(102−72)=51π\pi(10^2 - 7^2) = 51\piπ(102−72)=51π mm². The silver disc is 49π49\pi49π mm², so the difference is 2π2\pi2π mm², which is not among the options; the part is left out.

    Common trap: Part 3: using 3 mm as the outer radius. The gold ring is 3 mm wide, so the outer radius is 7+37 + 37+3.
